items.e: When a man betroths a woman, he debars himself from [marrying] seven blood relations, viz.: her mother, her mother’s mother, her father’s mother, her daughter, her son’s daughter, her daughter’s daughter and her sister while she herself is alive. In all these who are prohibited to him, the interdict is never lifted except in the case of his wife’s sister who is forbidden to him only during her lifetime; and never does he disqualify his wife [from cohabitation with him] through [his intercourse] with her mother, her daughter or her sister.

If [after betrothal the woman] was raped, she is permitted to him, but should she have been a willing party she is forbidden to him. If she is the wife of a kohen , she is forbidden to him whether [it happened] under force or with her consent. [For it is stated, And she be not seized —[only then] is she forbidden; if, however, she was seized she is permitted. There is another class of woman who is forbidden [to her husband] even though she had been seized; and who is that? The wife of a kohen . R. Ishmael said: And she be not seized she is forbidden; consequently if she had been seized she is permitted. There is another class of woman who is permitted [to her husband] even if she had not been seized; and who is that? A woman whose betrothal was mistaken.] If a divorcee who became betrothed was seduced, whether under force or of her free will, she is forbidden to return to her former husband. This is the opinion of R. Jose b. Ḳippar in the name of R. Eleazar b. Shammua‘. This is the reasoning by which R. Jose b. Ḳippar expounded his view: [It is written,] Her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled . In what circumstances did she become defiled? It can only be explained by what the Sages have said: If a woman [after betrothal] was forcibly seduced, she is permitted to [her husband]; if she was a willing party she is forbidden to him; but in this case, whether under compulsion or of her free will she is forbidden to return to her former husband.

None of the women forbidden to him on account of incest requires a geṭ from him if he married any of them except his wife’s sister, his brother’s wife and a married woman, because these have a termination to their prohibition.

The following exposition was given by R. Ḥanina b. Uri before [a gathering of] the Sages in the name of R. Nathan: Anyone who is included in the category Shall not enter [ into the assembly of the Lord ] disqualifies a woman by his cohabitation and disqualifies the child. They are: an Ammonite, Moabite, Egyptian, Idumean, slave, bastard, nathin , Samaritan and a ḥalal . The daughter of a ḥalal is fit although [her father] is within [the category of] shall not enter .

If a man had intercourse with any of the women prohibited to him as forbidden relatives, he is still permitted to marry her near relatives. [For instance,] he who had intercourse with a married woman is permitted to marry her daughter.

This is the question which R. Jose b. Taddai of Tiberias put to Rabban Gamaliel: If I, who may cohabit with my wife, am prohibited from marrying her daughter, how much more should I be prohibited from marrying the daughter of a married woman, seeing that I am prohibited from cohabiting with her! He replied to him: Go and provide me [a wife] for the High Priest of whom it is written, A virgin of his own people shall he take to wife , and I will provide you [with wives] for Israel. Another explanation [in refutation of the reasoning is that] we do not use an a fortiori argument to abrogate a specific law of Scripture. Rabban Gamaliel excommunicated him.

If a man cohabits with any woman forbidden him as incest, he does not thereby disqualify her from marrying a kohen . [If a kohen cohabits with his wife when she is] niddah , although he is liable to a penalty for the intercourse, the child [who is conceived] is qualified to stand and offer sacrifices upon the altar. A woman who had intercourse with that which is not a human being, although she is in consequence subject to the penalty of kareth , she is not disqualified from marrying a kohen . R. Jose said: It once happened at Haitali that while a young woman was cleaning the floor a gorilla came and covered her from the rear. When the case came before the Sages, they did not disqualify her from marrying a kohen .

The following are the forbidden relatives in the second degree: his father’s mother, his mother’s mother, the wife of his mother’s father, the wife of his father’s father, the wife of his son’s son, the wife of his daughter’s son, the wife of a father’s maternal brother, the wife of a mother’s paternal brother. Bar Ḳappara adds the mother of his father’s father and the mother of his mother’s father. The wife of his father’s brother is forbidden to him but the daughter [his cousin] is permitted to him; his father’s brother is permitted to marry his wife or his daughter; the wife of his mother’s brother is forbidden to him but his daughter is permitted to him. His mother’s brother is permitted to marry [the nephew’s] wife or daughter. A man is permitted to marry the wife of his father-in-law and the wife of his son-in-law, but the Sages said that the wife of his father-in-law is not permitted to him because of appearance’s sake; [the mother-in-law’s] daughter is permitted to him. A man may not marry the daughter of his stepson, but [the stepson’s] wife is permitted to him. His stepson is permitted to marry [the stepfather’s] wife and daughter. A man may marry the wife of his brother’s son and the wife of his sister’s son.

If a man remarried his divorced wife after her marriage [with a second husband who subsequently died or divorced her], he may not cohabit with her, neither may a levir marry her [if her husband died childless]. The wife of a fit man who has a brother who is crushed in his privy parts is permitted to her husband but is prohibited to the levir. The rival of a soṭah is permitted to her husband but forbidden to the levir. A man who married a sister of his brother’s divorced wife or a sister of his brother’s ḥaluẓah , [though this sister] is permitted to her husband she is forbidden to the levir [if her husband died childless]. The wife of a man crushed in his privy parts who has a fit brother, though forbidden to her husband, is permitted to the levir. A soṭah is forbidden both to the husband and to the levir. A ḥaluẓah is likewise forbidden to both. The wife of a man crushed in his privy parts whose brother is similarly maimed is forbidden to both.

A female proselyte, captive woman, freed woman, the widow of one who was of mixed family, a soṭah , [56 a ] ḥaluẓah , divorcee and a ḥalalah are unfit to marry a kohen . If they were married to a lay-Israelite, the daughters [of the union] are fit to marry a kohen .

He who cohabits with a maidservant is liable to the penalty for transgressing fourteen negative commands and also to the penalty of kareth at the hand of Heaven, viz.: Thou shalt not let thy cattle gender with a diverse kind; Thou shalt not sow thy field with two kinds of seed; Neither shall there come upon thee a garment of two kinds of stuff mingled together; Thou shalt not sow thy vineyard with two kinds of seed; Thou shalt not plough [ with an ox and an ass together ]; Thou shalt not wear a mingled stuff; Thou shalt not commit adultery; Thou shalt not covet; And thou shalt not lie with any beast; Neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God; also one on account of [laws concerning] a non-Jewish maidservant, a harlot, a niddah and a heathen woman. And one punishment of kareth , as it is stated, May the Lord cut off to the man that doeth this him that calleth and him that answereth out of the tents of Jacob, and him that offereth an offering unto the Lord of hosts . If he was a lay-Israelite and profaned his seed with a maidservant or a heathen woman, he will have no ‘awakening’ among the Sages and no ‘responding’ among the disciples. If he was a kohen , he will not have a son that offereth an offering unto the Lord of hosts .

Who marries a wife fitting for him; Elijah kisses and the Holy One, blessed be He, loves him; but who takes a wife who is not fitting for him, Elijah binds and the Holy One, blessed be He, lashes him. Woe to him who disqualifies his seed, blemishes his family and takes to wife one who is not fit for him. He who is himself unfit [continually] declares [others to be] unfit and never speaks well of anybody.

Abba Hilfai said in the name of his father Abba Ḥagra: Do not be rash in making vows that you may not trespass in the matter of oaths, and do not be the guest of a kohen who is an ‘am ha-’areẓ lest he give you consecrated food to eat. Do not converse much with women because every conversation with a woman is only about unchastity. R. Aḥi of the School of R. Josiah said: He who gazes at a woman eventually comes to sin, and he who looks upon a woman’s heel will beget degenerate children, and he who has no shamefacedness is easily led to sin; as it is stated, The show of their countenance doth witness against them [ and they declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not ]. But he who is shamefaced will not easily sin, as it is stated, [ And Moses said unto the people, fear not; for God is come to prove you ] that His fear may be before your face that ye sin not . R. Measha, grandson of R. Joshua b. Levi, said: One who looks at a naked part of the body and does not feed his eyes on it will merit to receive the Divine Presence; as it is stated, And [he that] shutteth his eyes from looking upon evil , and immediately after it is written, He shall dwell on high , and it is written, Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty .
Concerning Sadducees, informers, the wicked, profaners of God’s Name and heretics, Scripture declares, The wicked shall return to the nether-world .
Concerning the overbearing, haughty, proud, violent, insolent and pugnacious, Scripture declares, For the arms of the wicked shall be broken; but the Lord upholdeth the righteous .

Concerning designers of evil, schemers of [wicked] plans, those who spurn with their lips and the smooth-tongued, Scripture declares, Let their way be dark and slippery, the angel of the Lord pursuing them .

They who smite in secret, openly blaspheme, treat the public with contempt and causers of strife are destined to be like Ḳorah and his assembly, concerning whom Scripture declares, And the earth closed upon them, and they perished from among the assembly .

Concerning them who hoard fruit, raise the prices, make the ephah small and the shekel great and lend money on usury, Scripture declares, The Lord hath sworn by the pride of Jacob: Surely I will never forget any of their works .

The following do not bequeath anything to their children, and if they do bequeath to their children they do not cause their children’s children to inherit: the dice-gambler, the breeder of small cattle, one who transacts with money derived from the Sabbatical year, one whose money is derived from [transactions] with overseas countries and a kohen or Levite who borrowed on their portions.
Concerning flatterers, liars and workers of iniquity, Scripture declares, The wicked shall return to the nether-world , and it further states, That which is crooked cannot be made straight .

Concerning them who moan like a dove, who make motions with their hands [when talking], click their heels and walk on tip-toe, Scripture declares, Let not the foot of pride overtake me, and let not the hand of the wicked drive me away .
Concerning haughty men, purveyors of slander, them who use lewd language and them who are wise in their own eyes Scripture declares, For, behold, the day cometh, it burneth as a furnace .

Concerning him who takes a wife for his infant son, who marries his daughter to an old man and who does a favour to one without notifying him Scripture declares, The Lord will not be willing to pardon him .

Concerning tax-collectors, confiscators, extortioners and collectors of customs, Scripture declares, Thy riches, and thy wares, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the exchangers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that are in thee, with all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the heart of the seas in the day of thy ruin .

Concerning him who deceives his partner, who does not return a lost object to its owner, who lends money to his fellow with the object of foreclosing his house or his field, who indulges in perversion with his wife, and who lays wanton charges against his wife in order to divorce her, Scripture declares, I the Lord search the heart, I try the reins .

Concerning them who suffer insults but do not insult, who hear themselves reviled and do not answer back, who perform [religious precepts] from love and rejoice in their chastisements, Scripture declares, But they that love Him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might .

Concerning them who have a humble opinion of themselves, who are low in their own estimation, who subdue their [evil] inclination and who are humble of spirit, Scripture declares, Thus saith the Lord, the Redeemer of Israel, his Holy One, to him who is despised of men, to him who is abhorred of nations, to a servant of rulers: Kings shall see and arise, princes, and they shall prostrate themselves .

Concerning trustworthy men, them who keep a secret, who return a pledge and who restore a lost object [to its owner] Scripture declares, Mine eyes are upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me .

Concerning him who loves his wife as himself and honours her more than himself, who leads his children in the right path and marries his son just before he attains puberty, before he comes within the power of sin, Scripture declares, And thou shalt know that thy tent is in peace; and thou shalt visit thy habitation, and shalt not sin . Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be great, and thine offspring as the grass of the earth .

Concerning him who loves his fellow-men, who displays friendliness towards his relatives, who marries his sister’s daughter and lends a peruṭah to a poor man in the time of his need, Scripture declares, Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer .

Concerning them who confess their sins in earnestness, repent wholeheartedly, receive penitents and teach them to return from their sinful ways, Scripture declares, Then shall thy light break forth as the morning .

Concerning them who judge in righteousness, who reprove with sincerity, who perform [their daily tasks] in a state of [ritual] cleanliness and who are pure of heart, Scripture, declares, Surely God is good to Israel, even to such as are pure in heart .
Concerning them who sigh, grieve and look forward to [national] salvation and mourn for Jerusalem, Scripture declares, To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them a garland for ashes .
Concerning them who are merciful, who feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked and distribute alms Scripture declares, Say ye of the righteous, that it shall be well with him .

Concerning the poor, the bashful, the lowly of spirit, those who are gentle to the young and trustworthy men Scripture declares, Thou shalt also decree a thing, and it shall be established unto thee, and light shall shine upon thy ways .

Concerning them who toil in [propagating] the Torah, who study the Torah for its own sake, who are constantly in search of performing meritorious deeds and who wait for [the opening of the doors of] temples [of prayer and learning] Scripture declares, Happy is the man that hearkeneth to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at the posts of my doors .

Concerning them who pursue righteousness, who seek peace for their people, who grieve with the community and stand by them in the hour of their distress Scripture declares, The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and He knoweth them that take refuge in Him .

On account of four things is the sun in eclipse; on account of an ’Ab Beth Din who died and was not fittingly mourned; on account of a betrothed maiden who cried out aloud in the city and there was none to rescue her; on account of sodomy; and on account of two brothers whose blood was shed at the same time.

On account of four things are the luminaries in eclipse: on account of those who forge documents; on account of those who give false evidence; on account of those who breed small cattle; and on account of those who cut down good trees.

On account of four things the wealth of householders is confiscated by the government: on account of those who retain in their possession bills which have been paid; on account of those who lend money on usury; on account of those who had the power to protest [against wrongdoing] and failed to do so; and on account of those who publicly donate specified sums for charity and do not give them.

On account of four things is the property of householders appropriated by the State treasury: on account of those who withhold the hired labourer’s wages; on account of those who delay payment of the labourer’s wages; on account of those who remove the yoke from off their own neck and place it on their fellow-men; and [the sin of] arrogance is equal to them all.

R. Dosethai b. Judah said: One should always contend with the wicked, as it is stated, They that forsake the law praise the wicked; but such as keep the law contend with them . Should somebody whisper to you, ‘[But is it not written,] Contend not with evildoers, neither be thou envious against them that work unrighteousness? ’ answer him, ‘Only he whose conscience pricks him speaks thus. Contend not with evildoers means, to be like them; be not envious against them that work unrighteousness means, to emulate them’.
In the heavenly abode there is no sitting, eating, drinking, sleeping, procreation of children, enmity, hatred, rivalry, envy, obduracy, weariness or hindrance.

The same was said by David, king of Israel; for it is stated, He made darkness His hiding-place . With reference to whom did David say this verse? He only said it by way of praising the Holy One, blessed be He, Who is Yah ruling in the heights of the universe; He is One and His name is One, and He dwells in three hundred and ninety firmaments. Upon each firmament His Name and attributes are inscribed; in each are Ministering Angels, Seraphim, Ophannim, Cherubim, celestial spheres and the throne of glory. Do not wonder too much at this statement; because a king of flesh and blood has a number of residences, some for warm weather and some for cold weather; how much more so [can this be said] of the King, the Life of the universe, since everything belongs to Him! When Israel perform the will of the All-present, [56 b ] He dwells in Araboth the seventh [heaven] and He does not disinterest Himself in anything [in the world]; as it is stated, From between the two cherubim; and He spoke unto him . But when He is wroth, He ascends and dwells in the upper heavens, and though people cry aloud and weep, their voices are not heard, even though they decree a fast, wallow in ashes, clothe themselves in sackcloth and shed tears.

Ben ‘Azzai said: Whoever sets the following four things [constantly] before his eyes and upon his heart will never commit a sin: Whence he came, whither he goes, Who is his Judge and what he is destined to become. Whence he came? From a place of darkness. Whither he goes? To a place of thick darkness. [Another reading:] Whence he came? From a place of uncleanness. Whither he goes? To cause others to be unclean. [Another reading:] Whence he came? From a fetid drop and from a place which no person is able to behold. Whither he goes? To the nether-world to be judged in Gehinnom and burnt in fire. And Who is his Judge? He must realize that his Judge is not of flesh and blood but the Lord of all works, blessed be He, with Whom there is no injustice, forgetfulness, respect of persons or taking of bribes. What is he destined to become? A worm and maggot; as it is stated, How much less man, that is a worm! and the son of man, that is a maggot!
R. Simeon said: A man is [full of] worms during his life and [full of] maggots when dead. He is full of worms during life—i.e. vermin, and full of maggots when dead—i.e. what swarms when he is dead.

R. Eleazar b. Jacob said: Man is comely and praiseworthy but emits an ugly expression from his mouth. To what can this be compared? To a large salon in the middle of which a tannary pipe was fixed. So is man: if now when he discharges excrement from his bowels he prides himself over other creatures, should he emit from his bowels foliatum, balsam or any other kind of aromatic spice, how much more would he pride himself over other creatures!

Shortly before R. Eleazar b. Azariah died, his disciples went in to visit him. They sat in front of him and said, ‘Master, teach us the ways of life’. He said to them, ‘My sons, what can I teach you? Go and let each of you be solicitous for the honour of his colleague; and when you stand up to pray, know before Whom you stand and pray; for on that account you will [be worthy to] enter into the life of the World to Come’.

Five things we learnt from R. Eliezer at the time of his death, and we had greater joy over what we then learnt than over what he taught us during his life. They are: a ball, a shoe-last, an amulet, tefillin and a cushion can become unclean, and [if unclean] may be immersed just as they are. Go and pay due regard to them, because they are important ordinances which were told to Moses on Mount Sinai.

You should always be pleasant on entering and leaving [a house]. Spend less time on business and occupy yourself with [the study of] the Torah. It once happened that R. Simeon b. Eleazar was coming from Migdal Eder from the house of his teacher and was riding leisurely on his ass by the seaside. A certain man chanced to meet him, who was exceedingly ugly. He said to him, ‘Raḳa, how ugly are the children of Abraham our father!’ The other replied, ‘What can I do for you? Speak to the Craftsman Who made me’. R. Simeon b. Eleazar immediately dismounted from the ass, prostrated himself before him and said to him, ‘I apologize to you, forgive me’. He replied to him, ‘I will not forgive you until you go to the Craftsman Who made me and say to Him, “How ugly is the vessel which You have made!” ’ R. Simeon walked behind him for three mil . When his fellow-citizens heard [of his arrival] they came out to meet him, greeting him with the words, ‘Peace be upon you, Rabbi’. The man said to them, ‘Whom are you calling Rabbi?’ They answered, ‘He who is walking behind you’. Thereupon he exclaimed, ‘If this man be a Rabbi, may there not be any more like him in Israel!’ He told them the whole story. They earnestly begged him to pardon him, and he replied, ‘I will forgive him, but only on condition that he does not act in the same manner again’. That same day R. Simeon sat and expounded in his great Academy: Be always pliable like the reed and not unyielding like the cedar. In the case of a reed, though the four winds of the world were to blow upon it, the reed bends with them, and when the winds drop, it remains standing in its place, with the result that one is able to make a pen of it to write a scroll of the Torah. But the cedar is not like that: if the east, north [or] west wind blows upon it, it cannot move it from its place; but as soon as the south wind blows upon it, it uproots it and the result is that people come and cut it up, chop it and use it for building houses, and what is left is used for firewood. Therefore the Sages said: Be always pliable like the reed and not unyielding like the cedar.

How does one honour his teacher? When they are both walking along the way, he must place himself at his left hand and not at his right. If three [were walking together] and a Sage or a teacher was among them, the teacher is to be in the middle, the more important of the other two on his right and the less important on his left. We find it so in connection with the three angels who came to Abraham our father, viz. Gabriel, Michael and Raphael. Gabriel came to overthrow Sodom and Gomorrah, Raphael came to heal Abraham and Michael came to announce to Sarah [that she would have a son]. Michael was in the middle, Gabriel on his right and Raphael on his left. When Abraham our father saw the Ministering Angels, the Divine Presence appeared and stood over him. He said to them, ‘Sires, wait until I take leave of the Divine Presence, which is greater than you’, as it is stated, And he said: My lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant . When Abraham our father had taken leave of the Divine Presence, he came, bowed to them and led them beneath the tree, as it is stated, Let now a little water be fetched, and wash your feet , and afterwards [it is written], And I will fetch a morsel of bread . But [when the angels came] to Lot, what did he say? And tarry all night, and wash your feet . Others say: Lot spoke to them [in this manner] only as a clever device. He said [to himself], ‘If [the men of Sodom] find them with their faces, hands and feet already washed, the result will be that they will kill me, my wife and my daughters. Let them, therefore, find them with the dust still on their feet, and they will think that they have only just arrived’.

He who walks behind his teacher may not leave him without first obtaining his permission. If they were both equal in learning, the host enters [the house] first and then the guest, but when leaving the guest goes out first and the host leaves last. He who is about to leave the company of his fellow, whether he be greater than he or not, must say to him, ‘I am leaving’.

A person should never leave [the company of his teacher or even] his fellow unless he had previously obtained his consent. All can learn such good manners from the All-present, Who said, as it were, to Abraham, ‘I am now leaving’, as it is stated, And the Lord went His way , as soon as He had left off speaking to Abraham; and Abraham returned unto his place .

A person should never enter into someone else's house suddenly. And all people should learn derekh eretz (proper behavior) from the Omnipresent, Who stood at the entrance to the Garden [of Eden] and called to Adam, as it is stated, "And God called to Adam and said, 'Where are you?'" The story is told of the four Sages, viz. Rabban Gamaliel, R. Joshua, R. Eleazar b. Azariah and R. ‘Aḳiba, who were on their way to attend a Privy Council which also included a certain philosopher as a member. R. Joshua said to Rabban Gamaliel, ‘Master, would you like us to call on our companion the philosopher?’ He replied, ‘No’. In the morning he again asked him, ‘Master, would you like us to call on our companion the philosopher?’ He replied, ‘Yes’. R. Joshua went and knocked on the door. The philosopher thought and said [to himself], ‘This can only be the manners of a Sage’. [When he knocked] a second time, [the philosopher] got up and washed his face, hands and feet. On the third knock he arose and opened the door and saw the Sages of Israel coming all together. Rabban Gamaliel was in the middle, R. Joshua and R. Eleazar b. Azariah on his right and R. ‘Aḳiba on his left. The philosopher was meditating and saying [to himself], ‘How shall I greet these Sages of Israel? If I say, “Peace be upon you, Rabban Gamaliel”, I shall be guilty of derogatory conduct towards the [other] Sages. If I say, “Peace be upon you, Sages of Israel”, that would be an insult to Rabban Gamaliel’. As soon as he approached them, he greeted them with the words, ‘Peace be upon you, Sages of Israel, headed by Rabban Gamaliel’. (We learn [this rule of etiquette] not from [this story of] Rabban Gamaliel but from the Divine Presence, as it is stated, I saw the Lord sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right hand and on His left .)

Always let all people [who visit you] be regarded by you as robbers, but show them the same respect as to Rabban Gamaliel. The story is told of R. Joshua on whom a certain person called early in the morning. He gave him food and drink, and took him up to the loft to sleep and then removed the ladder from under him. What did that man do? He arose in the middle of the night, collected the vessels and wrapped them up in his cloak. As soon as he started to descend, he fell from the loft and broke his neck. When morning came, R. Joshua rose early and found him where he had fallen. He said to him, ‘Raḳa! do all persons act as you have?’ He replied, ‘Master, I did not know that you had removed the ladder from under me’. He said to him, ‘Raḳa! Do you not know that already yesterday we were suspicious of you?’ Hence R. Joshua said: Always let all men be in your eyes as robbers, but show them the same respect as to Rabban Gamaliel.

If one enters a house [by invitation], whatever the host tells him he must do. The story is told of R. Simeon b. Anṭipaṭros with whom many guests used to come and stay. When he pressed them to eat and drink, they vowed by the Torah that they would neither eat nor drink, but later they partook of food and drink. When the time came for them to depart he used to flagellate them. This matter came to the notice of Rabban Joḥanan b. Zakkai and the Sages who were angered by it. They said, ‘Who will go and inform us [of his action]?’ R. Joshua replied, ‘I will go and see how he conducts himself’. He went and found him at the entrance of his house and greeted him, ‘Peace be upon you, Master’. The other replied, ‘Peace be upon you, Master and Teacher’. He said, ‘I need a lodging’. The other replied, ‘Lodge here in peace’. They sat down and occupied themselves in the study of the Torah until evening. In the morning [R. Joshua] said to him, ‘Master, I want to go to the bath-house’. He replied, ‘As you wish’; whereupon R. Joshua was afraid lest he would smite him on his thighs. After he returned [from the bath-house] they ate and drank. He then said, ‘Who will accompany me [on my way back]?’ The other replied, ‘I will’. R. Joshua was then meditating and saying [to himself], ‘What can I report to the Sages who sent me [to institute inquiries]?’ He then turned [to look] back. [R. Simeon] asked him, ‘Master, why did you turn to look behind you?’ He replied, ‘I have something to ask you. Why did you flagellate other guests who stayed with you and me you did not flagellate?’ He said to him, ‘Master, you are a great Sage and you have good manners. The persons who stay with me I usually press to eat, but they vow by the Torah [not to eat] and transgress [their vow]; and so have I heard from the mouth of the Sages that whoever vows by the Torah and breaks his vow has to be given forty lashes’. He said to him, ‘May Heaven bless you for what you have done. By your life and by the life of your head! Whoever behaves in this manner, give him the forty lashes on your account [57 a ] and [another] forty on account of the Sages who sent me’. R. Joshua returned and reported to the Sages what he had witnessed while he was with Simeon b. Anṭipaṭros.

A man should never be fastidious concerning his meals. It once happened that Hillel the Elder had a certain man to a meal, when a poor person came and stood at his door and said, ‘I am to marry today and have no provisions at all’. Hillel’s wife took the entire meal [which she had prepared] and gave it to him. She then kneaded fresh dough, cooked another dinner and placed it before them. He said to her, ‘My dear, why did you not bring it to us sooner?’ She told him all that had happened. He said to her, ‘My dear, I, too, did not judge you in the scale of guilt but in the scale of merit, because everything you did was only in the name of Heaven’.

We do not leave over a portion of the food in a stew-pot, but we should leave over a portion of the food in the dish. It once happened that R. Joshua was the guest of a certain widow who served him with a dish of beans. He ate without leaving any. On the second occasion he also ate without leaving any. On the third occasion she over-seasoned it with salt; and as soon as R. Joshua tasted it he withdrew his hand from it and ate his bread dry. She asked, ‘Why did you withdraw your hand from the pounded beans?’ He replied, ‘I had already eaten earlier in the day’. She said to him, ‘You should then have withdrawn your hand also from the bread’. ‘Perhaps,’ she continued, ‘you left [the dish today] as compensation for the former meals! But have not the Sages said: We do not leave over a portion of the food in the stew-pot but we should leave over a portion of the food in the dish!’ Hence R. Joshua said, ‘No one has ever had the better of me except this woman, a little boy and a little girl’. What was the incident with the little girl? Once R. Joshua was walking in a field when he met a little girl who called out to him, ‘Why are you walking across the field?’ He replied, ‘I am walking along a [trodden] path’. ‘Robbers like yourself,’ she retorted, ‘have trodden it down.’ What was the incident with the little boy? Once R. Joshua was on a journey and came across a little boy sitting at a cross-road. He asked him, ‘My son, by which road will I be able to go to the town, by this one or by that?’ He replied, ‘Both of them are before you; but this one is long and short and that one is short and long’. [He proceeded along the short but long road.] When he approached the city’s wall, he found that it was surrounded by gardens and orchards, and turned back. Noticing the same little boy sitting where he had left him, he said, ‘My son, why did you play a trick on me? Did you not tell me that this road was short?’ ‘Master,’ he retorted, ‘you are a great Sage and this is your wisdom? Did I not tell you that it is long?’ R. Joshua went and kissed him upon his head and exclaimed, ‘Happy are you, O Israel, for all of you are wise, both young and old’.

How does one dance before a bride? Beth Shammai said, ‘The bride as she is’. Beth Hillel said, ‘Beautiful and graceful bride’. Beth Shammai said to Beth Hillel, ‘According to your view, if she were lame or blind one still has to call her “beautiful and graceful bride”, but the Torah has declared, Keep thee far from a false matter! ’ Beth Hillel replied to Beth Shammai, ‘If one has made a bad purchase in the market, should one praise it in his eyes or depreciate it? Surely one should praise it in his eyes’. Therefore the Sages said: The disposition of man should always be pleasant with people.

One should break off a piece of bread only from the part that is baked to a crust and not from the soft part; neither should one hold in his hand a piece [of bread] as big as an egg, because one who acts in this manner is a glutton and a tippler, neither should a man drink his goblet of wine in one draught, and if he did so he is a tippler and a glutton. How many pauses should he make before drinking it up? [If he drinks it] in two draughts he shows good manners; in three he is of the arrogant. A man should not begin to eat leek or onion from the top side but from the leaves, and if he did eat it so he is a glutton and a tippler. He should not drink two goblets for reciting Grace after meals because it makes him appear like a tippler.
When two sit at one table, the senior of them puts forth his hand first and then the junior; if the junior puts forth [his hand first] he is a glutton.

The story is told of R. ‘Aḳiba who prepared a meal for his disciples. They served them with two dishes, one raw and the other cooked. First they served them with raw foods. The bright [pupil] among them took hold of the stalk with one hand and with the other tried to break a piece off, and when it did not come off he withdrew his hands from it and ate his bread dry. The foolish [pupil], however, took hold of the stalk in one hand and bit into it with his teeth. R. ‘Aḳiba said to him, ‘Not so, my son; place your heel on it in the plate!’ After that a cooked dish was served to them, of which they ate their fill. Then [R. ‘Aḳiba] said to them, ‘My sons, I only did this to test whether you have good manners or not’.
A man should begin his mealtime at the fourth hour of the day and enter the bath-house only at the fourth hour of the day.
Hot baths in large quantities are harmful to the body and beneficial in small quantities; wine is harmful in large quantities and beneficial in small quantities.
The following three things are of equal importance, viz. wisdom, fear [of God] and humility.

When entering a privy one should not face west or east but only the sides. He should not expose himself until he sits, and should not wipe himself with the right hand but only with the left. It is related of R. ‘Aḳiba that he went into a privy behind R. Joshua to watch his behaviour. He noticed that he entered the privy only on the side, exposed himself only after he had sat down, and wiped himself only with the left hand. What is the reason that we do not wipe with the right hand? R. Eliezer said: Because one eats with it. R. Joshua said: Because one writes with it. Rabban Gamaliel said: Because one points with it to the cantillations of the Torah.

A man should not rejoice when among people who weep or weep when among those who rejoice. He should not stay awake among people who sleep or sleep when among those who are awake. He should not be standing when all others are sitting or sit when all others are standing. This is the general rule: A man should not deviate from the custom of his companions or from society.

A guest should not say to his host, ‘Serve me that I may eat’, but [must wait] until he is invited to eat. If they poured out a goblet [of wine] for him he must drink it with pauses. How many pauses should he make? In the case of warm [beverages] three and with cold four. R. Judah said: This applies only to goblets of Galilee, but with goblets used in Judah he drinks with as many pauses as he likes.

A man should not say to his fellow, ‘Come and eat [with me in return] for the food you gave me’, because this is a kind of usury. In Jerusalem, however, they used to exchange invitations one with another.

A man should not send to his fellow a barrel of wine and put oil at its mouth, because this may lead to fatal consequences. It once happened that a man arranged a banquet in honour of his son; when his guests arrived and sat down at the table, he went to get the oil. When he discovered that the barrel was full of wine he strangled himself and died. Hence the Sages said: A man should not send to his fellow a barrel of wine and put oil at its mouth, because it may lead to fatal consequences.

A man should not say to his fellow, ‘Take oil’ from an empty jar, because the latter would be grateful to him without cause. A man should not urge his fellow to dine with him knowing that he will not do so; and he should not offer him many gifts when he knows that he will not accept them.

A man should not pass off new wine for old when giving his friend a drink because that is a kind of robbery. If he was giving drink to ass-drivers, he may not say to them, ‘Take away this man’s cup and pass it to someone else’ because this is a kind of robbery.

If a man was standing by sellers of produce in a market-place, he may not say to them, ‘What is the price of this article?’ when he has no intention of buying it, because he encourages the mind of the seller [that he will sell it].

A man should not break bread over a dish, wipe the plate with a piece of bread, or gather the crumbs and leave them on the table, because such action is objectionable to men. One should not wipe the plate with a piece of bread and leave it on the table, because such action is objectionable to men. A man should not bite off a piece of bread and return it to the plate; similarly he should not bite off a piece of bread and give it to his fellow, because not all tastes are alike. He should also not drink from a cup and hand it to his fellow because of danger to life. Once R. ‘Aḳiba was staying at the inn of a certain man who handed him a goblet of wine from which he had already drunk. R. ‘Aḳiba said to him, ‘Take and drink it’. [The host] again handed him another goblet of wine from which he had previously drunk, and R. ‘Aḳiba said to him, ‘Take and drink it’. Ben ‘Azzai said to him, ‘How long will you give [R. ‘Aḳiba] goblets of wine which had previously been tasted!’

It is also related of R. ‘Aḳiba that he was staying at the inn of a certain man [57 b ] who took a piece of bread and used it to support his plate. R. ‘Aḳiba snatched [the bread] and ate it. [The innkeeper] said to him, ‘Master, have you no bread to eat other than that on which I rested the plate?’ He replied, ‘I imagined that you would be scalded with tepid water; but now [I see] that you are not scalded even with hot water’. A man should not drink his goblet and place it upon the table; but he should retain it until the waiter comes and then hand it to him.

Rabbi [Judah the Prince] said the following five things [concerning bread]: we may not place raw meat on bread, we may not pass a cup [full of wine] or a plate [of soup] over bread, we may not throw bread, we may not rest a dish on bread and we may not sit on articles of food because it would crush them. A guest may not take his portion and give it to the attendant, lest something untoward happen to [the rest of] the meal; but he should take [his portion], keep it in front of him and later hand it to the attendant.

Guests may not give anything [from what is set before them] to the host’s son or to his servant or deputy unless they have received the host’s permission to do so. It once happened that in a time of scarcity a man invited three guests to his house and only had three eggs which he set before them. When the host’s child entered and stood before them, one of the guests took his portion and gave it to him; the second guest did the same and so did the third. When the father came in and saw him with one egg in his mouth and holding two in his hands, he picked him up to his full height and flung him to the ground so that he died. When the mother saw her child dead she got up from [her seat] upon the roof and threw herself down and died. On seeing this, the father also stood on the roof and threw himself down and died. R. Eliezer b. Jacob said: Because of this three souls perished.

On entering a bath-house one should say, ‘May it be Thy will, O Lord my God, that Thou cause me to enter in peace and depart in peace, and that Thou cause me to return [to my house] in peace, and deliver me from this heat and its like in the future’. How should he conduct himself before entering? He removes his shoes, then his hat, then his cloak, then his girdle, then his shirt and finally his underwear. When he finished washing and left [the bath] and is handed a towel, he should dry his head and then the rest of his body. When he is given the oil he should oil his head and then the rest of his body. He then puts on his underwear and his shirt, binds his girdle, dons his cloak, [puts his hat on] and finally his shoes. [If he has his son with him or his servant, they put on the shoes for him.] He puts on the right [shoe] first and then the left, and when he removes them he takes the left off first and then the right. It is the same in connection with the tefillin: he puts on that of the hand first and then that of the head, and when he removes them he first takes off that of the head and then of the hand.

Who enters a bath-house should not knead or scrape or urinate on the marble floor. It once happened that they begged Rabban Gamaliel, who was weak, to urinate on the marble floor but he refused. Rabban Simeon b. Gamaliel said: He who urinates on the marble floor is the companion of an ass, and he who eats in the street is like a dog; some say that he is unfit to give evidence. In the case of a privy he who is inside must give way to him who enters; but in the case of a bath-house he who is about to enter must give way to him who is inside. One may not bring into the bath-house oil in a glass vessel because of danger. One may not spit in a bath-house because of danger. One may not spit anywhere in the presence of others.

One may cite the rules appertaining to a privy in a privy and the rules appertaining to a bath-house in a bath-house. One should not extend a greeting in a place where people are undressed but only in a place where the majority present are dressed. If most of the persons present are dressed it is as though they are all dressed; if the majority are undressed it is as though they are all undressed. A man may not give greeting to his fellow in the bath-house on account of danger, and if one does greet him he should say, ‘It is a bath-house!’ Others say that he may return the greeting and it does not matter.

A man should not let his feet [dangle] in a bath-tub while he lies stretched out [naked], because it is immodest. A man should not say to his fellow in a bath-house, ‘Rub me in well with your hand’, and he who says so will not depart from there unscathed. R. Judah said: This only applies when there is little water, but when there is plenty of water it is all right. It is discreditable for a man to read [the Shema‘ ] twice or to immerse [in a ritual bath] twice.

If a man covers himself in his cloak and stays in the room where they sweat he is as if he robbed the public. He who washes himself in cold water and then sluices himself with lukewarm water is as if he robbed the public. And if one did rob the public what should he do? He should go and dig wells, ditches and grottoes, or repair highways and streets, and then he will be forgiven.

If one starts out on a journey alone before cock-crow his blood is upon his head. R. Josiah said: [He should wait] until [the cock] crowed at least twice. What kind of cock? The average type, as it is stated, Who hath put wisdom in the inward parts? or who hath given understanding to the coc?
If [immediately] on returning from a journey a man enters a bath-house, undergoes cupping, has marital intercourse and sleeps on the floor, his blood is upon his head.
If one kills a louse upon his bed, or stands naked in front of a candle-light or in the moonlight, his blood is upon his head.
[He who eats peeled garlic, a peeled egg or a peeled onion which were kept overnight] and he who drinks diluted liquids or uncovered water which were kept overnight, his blood is upon his head.

[One may not sit at his table under an olive-tree on account of danger.] He who drinks water from brooks, rivers or pools [direct] with his mouth or by [drawing the water] with one hand, his blood is upon his head because leeches are there.
If a man observes a fast after letting blood, his blood is upon his head.

They who write scrolls [of the Torah], tefillin and mezuzoth , they, their traders and traders’ traders will never see a sign of blessing [from their earnings]. [They who deal in ritually unclean food and forbidden fat will never see a sign of blessing.]
He who trades in canes and jars will never see a sign of blessing.
One who does work on the Ninth of Ab will never see a sign of blessing [in the work he does on that day]. R. ‘Aḳiba said: Scholars should abstain from work [on that day].
They who cut down [beautiful] trees, breeders of small cattle, and they who trade on market-stands will never see a sign of blessing.
Anyone who sells his scroll [of the Torah] though he does not require it, or sells his daughter [to be a handmaid] though he has no food, will never see a blessing [from that money].

R. Isaac said: Slanderers are like shedders of blood, as it is stated, Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people; neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour . R. Eliezer said: He who hates his fellow belongs to the shedders of blood, as it is stated, If any man hate his neighbour, and lie in wait for him, and rise up against him, and smite him , etc. Ben ‘Azzai said: He who hates his wife belongs to the shedders of blood, as it is stated, And if he lay wanton charges against her , with the consequence that he hires [false] witnesses and has her hastily brought to the place of stoning. R. Jose said: He who calculates the end has no portion in the World to Come. He who hates Sages and their disciples, a false prophet and he who spreads calumny have no portion in the World to Come.

R. Meir said: Whoever has a House of Study in his town and does not frequent it forfeits his life, as it is stated, Thus saith the Lord: What unrighteousness have your fathers found in Me that they are gone far from Me? How much more so [if he does not attend] an Academy which contains thousands and myriads of Biblical precepts! R. Meir said: Anyone who has a scholar near him and does not wait upon him [as a disciple] forfeits his life, as it is stated, Because he hath despised the word of the Lord .

Anyone who goes into the street with his shoes unlaced is haughty of spirit. [He who walks] with his sanṭer hanging side-ways, or his cap turned backwards, or [sits] crosslegged, or holds in his hand the straps of the tefillin and puts them back while walking in the street belongs to the haughty of spirit. Every man in whom there is haughtiness of spirit is as though he worships idols, as it states, Thou shalt not bring an abomination into thine house , and it states elsewhere, Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the Lord: the word abomination is written in the one connection and also in the other—as the abomination mentioned in the one refers to idolatry so the abomination mentioned in the other refers to idolatry.

On going to bed one says, ‘Blessed … Who causeth [58 a ] the bands of sleep to fall upon my eyes’, and on waking he says, ‘O my God, the soul which Thou hast given me is pure’. On turning on his side from his sleep he says, ‘Blessed … Who looseneth the bound’.

On entering a privy one should say, ‘Be honoured, ye honoured and holy beings who minister to the Most High! Give glory to our God and stay where you are. Help me, guard me, support me and wait for me until I enter and come out, for this is the way of human beings’. On leaving a privy one says, ‘Blessed is He Who has formed man in wisdom’. When he has washed his face he says, ‘Blessed … Who removest the bands of sleep from my eyes and slumber from my eyelids’.

When he is clothed and goes out into the street he should say, ‘May it be Thy will, O Lord my God, that Thou conduct me in peace and uphold me in peace; and let me obtain grace, favour and mercy in Thine eyes and in the eyes of all who behold me; bestow lovingkindnesses upon me, and cause me to return to my house in peace. Deliver me from the hand of every enemy and ambush by the way and from an evil tongue. Let me not become accustomed to sin, transgression or iniquity, and let me not err in a matter of halakah or in any matter whatsoever. Deliver me from all kinds of harm and from all manner of afflictions which break forth and come upon the world that they do not injure me by day or by night. Blessed is He Who bestoweth lovingkindnesses upon His people Israel’. May it be the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, that He cause us to behold the rejoicing and comfort of Jerusalem, Amen.
